topical: High-potency Steroids (Clobetasol or Betamethasone) for hands and feet.
Calamine Lotion: To soothe itching and dry up weeping blisters.
Barrier Creams: To protect the skin from further contact.
oral: Increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma (cancer) in chronic erosive oral cases.
key_features: Tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin. Usually found on the abdomen, groin, and inner thighs/arms.
differential_diagnosis: Distinguish from Pemphigus Vulgaris (flaccid blisters/baki), Cicatricial Pemphigoid, and Bullous Impetigo.
emergency: If redness spreads rapidly or signs of fever appear, seek IV antibiotics immediately.
injectable: Intralesional Steroid (Triamcinolone): Injected into an inflamed (but not infected) cyst to shrink it quickly.
common_locations: Anywhere an injury or rash occurred (Face, back, legs).
topical_creams: Low-potency Corticosteroids (Desonide) - for short-term use on the face
Pimecrolimus (Elidel) - Non-steroidal cream for sensitive areas
shampoo_use: Apply medicated shampoo to the scalp, leave it for 5-10 minutes before rinsing. Use 2-3 times a week.
treatment: Apply steroid cream 2 times daily for up to 2 weeks. Avoid the trigger substance strictly.
common_triggers: Nickel (in jewelry), Fragrances, Latex, Harsh detergents, and certain plants.
adult: Requires immediate surgical consultation. Treatment plans are highly individualized by an Oncologist.
senior: Monitor for skin thinning. Check for interactions between systemic psoriasis drugs and heart medications.
physical: Contractures (difficulty moving arms or legs due to scarring), Lymphoedema, and rarely, Skin Cancer (SCC) in chronic scars.
psychological: Lowered self-esteem, especially when PIH covers large areas of the face.
dark_skin_presentation: Must be distinguished from 'Melanonychia' (dark lines in the nail), which can be a sign of Melanoma in dark-skinned individuals.
pediatric: Sun protection must start from birth. Use clothing as the primary barrier.
skin: Post-inflammatory Hyperpigmentation (dark spots that remain after the rash heals, especially in dark skin).
hair: Lichen Planopilaris (permanent hair loss if it affects the scalp).
christmas_tree_pattern: The long axis of the oval spots follows the lines of the ribs on the back.
pregnancy_warning: Consult a doctor; many rosacea treatments are not safe during pregnancy.
ocular: Permanent eye damage if Ocular Rosacea is not treated.
topical_therapy: High-potency Clobetasol Propionate cream: Applied to the whole body (very effective for localized cases).
systemic_oral: Oral Antibiotics: Combination of Clindamycin and Rifampicin (for severe cases).
Hormonal therapy: Spironolactone or birth control pills for women.
Metformin: Sometimes used to help reduce inflammation even if the patient isn't diabetic.
biologics_injectables: Adalimumab (Humira): The first FDA-approved biologic for moderate-to-severe HS.
social: Severe pain, foul-smelling discharge leading to social isolation and work absenteeism.
oral_medications: Antibiotics (Dicloxacillin or Cephalexin): Only if the cyst becomes infected (red, hot, and painful).
NSAIDs (Ibuprofen): To reduce pain and swelling.
rupture: If the cyst pops inside the skin, it causes a severe inflammatory reaction (feels like a massive boil).
recurrence: The condition is unpredictable; hair may fall out and grow back several times in a lifetime.
skin_damage: Ochronosis (permanent blue-black soot-like pigmentation) if high-strength Hydroquinone is used for too long without a break.
permanence: Dermal PIH (deep pigment) may take years to fade or may never fully disappear without professional intervention.
malignancy: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) - The most common and dangerous skin cancer in Albinism.
solar_elastosis: Prematurely wrinkled, thick, and leathery skin from sun damage.
dark_skin_context: In African communities, Albinism is very prominent, and the sun damage often presents as 'freckles' (Ephelides) which are early signs of UV stress.
advanced_treatments: Immunotherapy: Drugs like Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) or Nivolumab that help the immune system fight the cancer.
Targeted Therapy: Vemurafenib or Dabrafenib (for cancers with the BRAF gene mutation).
Chemotherapy: Rarely used today as first-line treatment due to better options.
metastasis: Spreading to the lungs, liver, or brain (associated with high mortality).
clinical_assessment: Dermoscopy to visualize 'leaf-like areas', 'large blue-gray ovoid nests', and 'arborizing telangiectasias'.
biopsy_techniques: Shave biopsy for superficial lesions; Punch biopsy or incisional biopsy for thicker or recurrent lesions.
imaging: CT or MRI for large tumors (>2cm) to check for perineural invasion or bone destruction.
topical_agents: Imiquimod 5% Cream: Immune response modifier used for small, superficial BCCs.
5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) 5%: Topical antimetabolite for multiple superficial lesions.
targeted_systemic_therapy: Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitors: Vismodegib (Erivedge) or Sonidegib (Odomzo) for metastatic or locally advanced BCC not amenable to surgery or radiation.
local_destruction: Destruction of facial structures like the nose (columella), eyelids, and pinna of the ear.
perineural_invasion: The cancer grows along nerves, causing severe pain, numbness, or facial paralysis.
recurrent_disease: Incomplete excision leads to recurrence, often with more aggressive histology.
physical_examination: Assessment for subungual hyperkeratosis (debris under nail), onycholysis (nail lifting), and thickening.
biopsy_protocol: Deep punch biopsy or incisional biopsy to evaluate the depth of invasion (Breslow thickness) and histological grade (Well-differentiated vs. Poorly differentiated).
lymph_node_assessment: Palpation of regional lymph nodes (neck, armpits, groin). Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) if nodes are suspicious.
topical_chemotherapy: 5-Fluorouracil (Efudix): Blocks DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cancer cells (Used only for early, non-invasive SCC).
Imiquimod (Aldara): A toll-like receptor 7 agonist that stimulates the immune system to destroy tumor cells.
systemic_immunotherapy: Cemiplimab (Libtayo): A PD-1 inhibitor for patients with metastatic SCC or locally advanced SCC who are not candidates for surgery.
Pembrolizumab (Keytruda): Another immunotherapy option for advanced cases.
physical_palpation: Tactile examination is essential; AKs often feel like 'sandpaper' or 'grittiness' even if they are not fully visible.
dermoscopy: Looking for 'red-to-blue lacunae' (well-defined rounded structures) which are diagnostic for vascular lesions.
skin_biopsy: Required if the lesion becomes thick, tender, bleeds, or grows rapidly to rule out invasive SCC.
topical_antimetabolites: 5-Fluorouracil (Efudix) 5% Cream: The gold standard for treating large areas ('field cancerization'). It kills precancerous cells by blocking DNA synthesis.
Diclofenac Sodium 3% Gel: A milder topical treatment used for 60-90 days.
immune_response_modifiers: Imiquimod (Aldara) 5% Cream: Stimulates the local immune system to recognize and destroy the abnormal cells.
Tirbanibulin (Klisyri): A newer, short-course treatment (5 days) that disrupts microtubule formation in cancer cells.
malignant_transformation: Small percentage can evolve into Melanoma.
field_cancerization: When a whole area (like the scalp) has sub-clinical damage, leading to multiple new AKs over time.
cosmetic_disfigurement: Chronic crusting, redness, and scarring if left untreated.
clinical_inspection: Searching for violaceous (purple) or reddish-brown lesions on the skin, mucosa, and hard palate.
histopathology: Skin biopsy showing spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells.
systemic_screening: HIV ELISA/Western Blot test (Mandatory); Chest X-ray to check for pulmonary KS; Endoscopy for GI involvement if abdominal pain is present.
cd4_count_and_viral_load: To assess the level of immune suppression.
antiretroviral_therapy_art: The cornerstone for AIDS-related KS. HAART helps the immune system recover, which can lead to spontaneous regression of the tumors.
systemic_chemotherapy: Liposomal Doxorubicin (Doxil): The first-line treatment for advanced or symptomatic KS.
Paclitaxel: Used as a second-line therapy for resistant cases.
topical_and_intralesional: Alitretinoin Gel: For localized skin lesions.
Intralesional Vinblastine: Injecting chemotherapy directly into the tumor (for small, localized spots).
visceral_involvement: Spreading to the lungs (causing cough and breathing difficulty) or GI tract (causing bleeding).
lymphedema: Severe swelling of the legs or face because the tumor blocks the lymph nodes.
secondary_infections: Ulcerated lesions can become infected with bacteria.
ugly_duckling_sign: Comparing one mole to others on the body to see if it stands out as abnormal.
biopsy: Scalp biopsy may be done if the diagnosis is unclear to rule out scarring alopecia.
psychological_distress: Especially if the mole is large or on a prominent part of the face.
irritation: Can be nicked during shaving (especially on the legs), leading to recurrent bleeding.
topical_treatment: Hydrogen Peroxide 40% (Eskata): An FDA-approved concentrated solution for clearing raised SKs (used in-clinic).
Ammonium Lactate or Alpha Hydroxy Acids (AHAs): To help soften and reduce the thickness of the lesions.
psychological_impact: Cosmetic concern when they appear in large numbers on the face or chest.
misdiagnosis: Mistaking it for Melanoma or Basal Cell Carcinoma due to dark pigmentation.
note: Medical treatment is generally not required unless the lesion is symptomatic.
topical_steroids: May occasionally be used if the nodule is very itchy or inflamed, though they won't remove it.
cosmetic_concern: Persistent dark spot that may be mistaken for a mole or cancer.
scarring: The scar from removal is often more noticeable than the nodule itself.
diascopy: Pressing a glass slide against the lesion to see if the blood empties from the vessels.
ultrasound_doppler: Used for deep hemangiomas to assess blood flow and depth.
infantile_specific: Propranolol (Oral): The gold standard for growing Infantile Hemangiomas; it helps shrink the vessels.
Timolol Maleate (Topical): A beta-blocker gel used for superficial, thin hemangiomas.
topical_for_adults: No effective topical cream to remove Cherry Angiomas; physical removal is required.
hemorrhage: Spontaneous bleeding if the lesion is bumped or scratched (especially Pyogenic Granuloma).
ulceration: The surface can break down, leading to pain and potential infection.
visual_impairment: If located on the eyelid, it can cause amblyopia (lazy eye) or vision loss.
trichoscopy: Using a dermoscope to see 'Exclamation point hairs' (hairs that are thinner at the base), 'yellow dots', and 'black dots'.
blood_tests: Checking for Thyroid (TSH) and ANA (Lupus) levels as it often co-occurs with other autoimmune issues.
first_line_treatment: Intralesional Corticosteroids (Triamcinolone): Injections directly into the bald patches every 4-6 weeks (Most effective).
Topical High-Potency Steroids: Clobetasol propionate cream or foam for children or those who fear needles.
second_line_treatment: Minoxidil (Rogaine) 5%: Used to stimulate hair regrowth after the inflammation is controlled.
Anthralin: A synthetic tar-like substance that irritates the skin to trigger hair growth.
advanced_therapy: JAK Inhibitors (Baricitinib): A newer, FDA-approved oral medication for severe, universal alopecia.
regrowth_pattern: Hair often regrows white or fine (vellus) at first before returning to its original color.
spontaneous_remission: Up to 50% of patients with mild patchy disease recover within one year without treatment.
potassium_hydroxide_koh_test: Scraping debris from under the nail and looking at it under a microscope to find fungal hyphae.
fungal_culture: To identify the exact species of fungus (takes 2-4 weeks).
nail_biopsy_pas_stain: The most accurate test; a piece of the nail is sent to the lab for special staining.
oral_antifungals: Terbinafine (Lamisil): The first-line treatment. Dose: 250mg daily for 6 weeks (fingernails) or 12 weeks (toenails).
Itraconazole (Sporanox): Used in 'pulse therapy' (one week on, three weeks off).
topical_lacquers: Ciclopirox (Penlac) 8%: Applied daily like nail polish; effective for mild cases.
Efinaconazole (Jublia): A newer topical with better penetration into the nail plate.
warning_note: Oral antifungals require monitoring of liver enzymes (LFTs) before and during treatment.
secondary_infection: Staphylococcus aureus infection of the raw areas.
permanent_nail_dystrophy: The nail may never grow back normally if the matrix is damaged.
pain_and_discomfort: Difficulty walking or wearing shoes due to thickened nails.
immediate_action: Discontinue the offending drug immediately. This is the single most important step.
hospital_treatment: Intravenous Fluids: For massive fluid loss (like a burn victim).
Cyclosporine: To suppress the immune attack on the skin.
IVIG (Intravenous Immunoglobulin): To neutralize the cell death process.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Controversial but used in very early stages.
sepsis: Bacterial infection of the blood due to loss of skin barrier.
organ_failure: Acute kidney injury or respiratory failure.
death: Mortality rate is approximately 5-10% for SJS.
mucosal_involvement: Hemostatic crusting (bloody crusts) on the lips is a hallmark.
systemic_therapy: Doxycycline: Often combined with Nicotinamide for its anti-inflammatory effects.
Immunosuppressants: Azathioprine or Mycophenolate Mofetil to reduce steroid side effects.
steroid_side_effects: Diabetes, hypertension, and osteoporosis in elderly patients due to long-term treatment.
dehydration: Loss of fluids through the blistered areas.
